title: Recording Old Red for Decca and losing the royalties
summary: He composed many Hamfats tunes. The band auditioned at Decca with Old Red, recorded it despite his advice to get a contract, made up Lake Providence Blues in the studio, and received no royalties.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well, Herb, weren't you directly responsible for the formation of the Harlem Ampets? Yeah. And didn't you write a great many of the tunes?
Yeah, a great many of them, yeah.
But you didn't, you didn't get much royalty from Decca from that, did you? No, no.

Decca, like Old Red, was a, was a hit. I went down to Decca Studios to make a, to have an audition. Let them hear the band. Well, at that time, all the boys was anxious to record and everything. So we played Old Red for an audition number and they decided to record it. Well, Joe McCoy and myself, he's the one that sings Old Red, and just called, you know, formed a band together, him and I. And I told them it would be a wrong move to, to do any recording without a contract or anything. So they all decided to go on and record it, so there's nothing I could do. So we recorded Old Red, so they asked us another number to put on the other side. And we made up a blues right in the studio, Lake Providence Blues. While we recorded that in about a month, all over Chicago, Old Red, what you gonna do?
And following, following that you recorded some other tunes that were equally successful. Right.

And this one part I want to say, that song made a lot of money for everybody but the Hollabamparts. If they just had to act fair with us, we would have got a nice piece. So they kept all the royalties. We didn't get nothing.
